title: Requirements to Executable Specifications and Code Generation · Iterative Development and Loop Engineering

slides.title: Spec‑Driven Development Recap
slides.notes: Remind students that Week 5 introduced spec‑driven development: requirements are expressed as executable specifications that can be run as tests. This shifts verification left and makes later AI‑assisted generation reliable. Emphasize the contract between spec and implementation — every public method must satisfy its spec.

slides.title: From Requirements to Executable Specs
slides.notes: Show how a natural‑language requirement is decomposed into concrete, testable scenarios. Each scenario becomes an executable specification that defines the exact interface contract for a public method. Stress traceability: every requirement line maps to at least one spec.

slides.title: Writing Executable Specifications
slides.notes: Walk through the pipeline: a requirements document is parsed, each user story is turned into Given/When/Then steps, pre‑ and post‑conditions are made explicit, and a schema validator ensures completeness. This pipeline is the foundation for later code generation — the spec is the single source of truth.

slides.title: Example: Requirement → Spec
bullets: Requirement: "User can withdraw cash if balance sufficient"
Covers happy path and insufficient‑funds path

figure.caption: Gherkin spec for cash withdrawal
figure.code:
Feature: Cash withdrawal
  Scenario: Sufficient balance
    Given the account balance is $100
    When the user requests $60
    Then the dispenser provides $60
    And the account balance becomes $40
  Scenario: Insufficient balance
    Given the account balance is $30
    When the user requests $60
    Then the transaction is rejected
    And the account balance remains $30

slides.notes: Present the two scenarios side‑by‑side. Highlight that each step maps directly to a method contract (e.g., `withdraw(amount) -> Result`). The spec is executable: a test runner can invoke the system under test and verify the post‑conditions automatically.

slides.title: Worked Problem: Translate Requirement to Spec & Generate Code
bullets: Step 4: Prompt AI model for implementation
Step 5: Run generated tests against spec

figure.caption: Generated Python withdrawal method

slides.notes: Demonstrate the full translation live: start from the textual requirement, produce the Gherkin spec (as in previous slide), infer the `withdraw` signature, feed the spec to an AI coding agent, and show the generated implementation. Run the spec‑driven test suite to confirm the code meets every scenario. This models the skill assessed in CO2.LO2.

slides.title: AI‑Assisted Code Generation from Specs
bullets: Iterate on failures via feedback loop
slides.notes: Explain how modern systems (e.g., AlphaCode) treat the executable spec as a prompt, ask a large language model for code, then automatically run the spec’s test suite. Failures are fed back as additional context for a repair iteration. Cite the AlphaCode paper for the competition‑level results.

slides.title: Check: Spec‑Driven Concepts

quiz.question: Which artifact is the single source of truth for the expected behavior of a public method in spec‑driven development?
quiz.explanation: The executable specification (e.g., Gherkin scenarios) is the authoritative, runnable contract. The implementation must satisfy it; the requirements document is higher‑level and not directly executable.

slides.notes: Quick poll to verify students grasp that the spec, not the code, defines the contract. The most tempting wrong answer is the requirements document because it originates the spec.

slides.title: Iterative Loop Engineering Recap
bullets: Agents produce code, tests, and logs
slides.notes: Briefly recap the iterative loop engineering cycle introduced in the previous week. Emphasize that the loop is driven by execution logs, which capture every control‑flow decision made by the coding agent. This sets the stage for trace analysis (CO3.LO1).

slides.title: Loop Engineering Phases
bullets: Execute: run in sandbox, collect logs
Reflect: analyse logs, decide next step

figure.caption: Four phases of an engineering loop

slides.notes: Detail each phase. In Plan, the human or a planner agent states the objective (e.g., implement `withdraw`). Generate invokes the coding agent. Execute runs the code in an isolated environment, producing a structured log. Reflect parses the log to detect errors, performance issues, or spec violations, then feeds insights back to Plan.

slides.title: Execution Logs and Tracing
bullets: Logs record every function call, branch, exception
Structured format: timestamp, thread, event, payload
slides.notes: Show a concrete log line. Explain that each entry captures a control‑flow step (call, return, branch, exception). The structured schema makes it possible to reconstruct the full execution trace automatically, which is essential for the tracing skill in CO3.LO1.

slides.title: Example: Annotated Execution Log
bullets: Log shows successful withdrawal then retry

figure.caption: Annotated log excerpt
figure.code:
[INFO] CALL withdraw(amount=60)   # spec: sufficient balance
[INFO] RETURN ok balance=40          # post‑condition met
[WARN] CALL withdraw(amount=60)   # spec: insufficient balance
[ERROR] RETURN fail "Insufficient funds"  # expected failure
[INFO] REFLECT: all scenarios passed

slides.notes: Walk through the annotated log line by line. Show how the spec’s Given/When/Then checkpoints appear as comments. The log demonstrates that the agent exercised both scenarios and the reflection step confirmed compliance. This models the tracing activity required for CO3.LO1.

slides.title: Worked Problem: Trace Log to Find Failure
bullets: Identify control‑flow steps for each scenario
Locate the first deviation from spec
Classify failure cause: logic, env, spec mismatch
Record evidence (log lines) for each cause

figure.caption: Log snippet with injected bug
figure.code:
[INFO] CALL withdraw(amount=60)
[INFO] BRANCH balance>=amount? false   # bug: condition reversed
[ERROR] RETURN fail "Insufficient funds"
[INFO] REFLECT: scenario 1 failed

slides.notes: Present a log where the agent incorrectly implements the balance check (condition reversed). Guide students to trace the BRANCH event, compare with the spec’s pre‑condition, and classify the failure as a logic error. Emphasize recording the exact log lines as evidence — this is the core of CO3.LO1.

slides.title: Check: Loop Engineering & Tracing

quiz.question: In an iterative loop engineering log, which event type most directly reveals a branch decision that caused a spec violation?
quiz.explanation: BRANCH events record the outcome of conditional statements. A mismatch between the expected branch (per spec) and the logged branch pinpoints the exact control‑flow deviation. CALL/RETURN show entry/exit but not the decision.

slides.notes: Reinforce that BRANCH entries are the key to tracing control‑flow errors. The distractor RETURN is tempting because it shows the result, but it does not expose the decision logic.

slides.title: Hands‑On: Write Spec, Run Agent, Inspect Log
bullets: Pair up: each pair gets a tiny requirement
Invoke coding agent via provided API
Identify any spec violations and classify causes
slides.notes: Students apply the full pipeline: requirement → spec → AI generation → log tracing. TAs circulate to help with the agent API and log format. The activity directly practices CO2.LO2 (spec authoring and code generation) and CO3.LO1 (log tracing and failure classification). Allocate 12 minutes; pairs submit annotated logs for quick review.

slides.title: Summary: Specs, Generation, and Loop Engineering
bullets: Executable specs are the contract for every public method
AI agents generate code from specs; tests close the loop
Iterative loops: plan → generate → execute → reflect
Structured logs enable full control‑flow tracing
slides.notes: Recap the two pillars of the lecture. First, spec‑driven development turns vague requirements into runnable contracts that guide AI code generation. Second, iterative loop engineering uses execution logs to observe, diagnose, and repair agent behavior. Both skills are assessed in Assignment 3 and the mid‑semester exam.
